draft.title: Weathering
card: Weathering is the breaking down of rock where it sits. The broken rock is not carried away while it is being weathered.
Physical
rock is broken into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of. Heating and cooling, and water freezing in cracks, can split rock apart.
Chemical
rock is changed or dissolved by a chemical reaction, such as rainwater slowly reacting with it. This can change what the rock is made of.
Biological
living things help break rock down. Plant roots grow into cracks and can widen them over time.
draft.remember: Weathering breaks rock down in place, by physical, chemical or biological processes.

a.q: Water seeps into a crack in a rock and freezes. The ice widens the crack. What kind of weathering is this?
a.why: Freezing water splits the rock into pieces without changing what it is made of, so it is physical weathering. It is not biological, because no living thing is involved.
a.clue: The rock is split, but not changed into something else.

b.q: A tree seedling grows in a crack in a sandstone cliff. Years later, its roots have widened the crack. What kind of weathering is this?
b.why: The roots of a living plant are breaking the rock, so this is biological weathering. Physical weathering is tempting because the crack is forced wider, but the cause here is a living thing.
b.clue: Ask what is doing the breaking.

problems.detail: Root wedging breaks rock into pieces without changing what it is made of, which fits the card's own definition of physical weathering. Many textbooks call it physical (mechanical) weathering caused by a living thing, so 'Physical weathering' is defensible alongside 'Biological weathering'. Reword the question to ask which of the card's three types the living cause points to, or replace 'Physical weathering' with a clearly wrong option.
